author: Kenji Watanabe
content:
# ADR-019: Migrate notifications and inventory to the event bus

**Status:** Accepted. **Migration date:** 5 August 2026.

## Context

The Notification Service currently depends on an HTTP webhook from the Order Service. When the notifier is slow, the Order Service blocks, and webhook calls are lost during deploys.

## Decision

On 5 August 2026:

- The Notification Service will consume order events from the Event Bus instead of the webhook. The webhook will be disabled the same day.
- The Inventory Service will start publishing stock-changed events to the Event Bus.

## Consequences

- Event volume on the cluster is expected to roughly double. Capacity should be reviewed after the migration.
- Consumers must be idempotent because the bus guarantees at-least-once delivery.
title: ADR-019: Migrate notifications and inventory to the event bus

author: Tomasz Wierzbicki
content:
# ADR-014: Move fraud scoring into the payment flow

**Status:** Accepted. **Effective:** 1 June 2026.

## Context

Today the Checkout API calls the Fraud Scoring Service directly before payment and ignores missing scores. This means non-checkout payments (subscriptions, phone orders) are never scored, and the Payments Team cannot enforce fraud decisions.

## Decision

From 1 June 2026 the Payments API will call the Fraud Scoring Service before every authorization. Checkout will stop calling fraud scoring in the same release window (Checkout API v5.3.0, Payments API v2.9.0).

## Consequences

- Fraud scoring becomes a hard dependency of payments; its latency adds directly to authorization time.
- The timeout and fail-open policy must be agreed before launch.
- Fraud scoring keeps using account-age signals from the Accounts Service.
title: ADR-014: Move fraud scoring into the payment flow

author: Priya Raman
content:
# Checkout architecture overview

_Last reviewed: 3 April 2026. Owner: Checkout Team._

## Purpose

The checkout subsystem turns a cart into a paid order. It is the most revenue-critical path in Kestrel Commerce and every component on it is tier 1 or tier 2.

## Request flow

A checkout request enters through the API Gateway and is handled by the Checkout API (co-api). The Checkout API is owned by the Checkout Team.

1. co-api validates the customer's session token with the Auth Service on every step.
2. It loads the basket from the Cart Service. The Cart Service itself asks the Pricing Engine for line prices, and stores carts in Shared Redis.
3. Checkout asks the Pricing Engine for the final price, promotions and taxes. Pricing reads product data from the Catalog Service.
4. Stock is checked and reserved through the Inventory Service.
5. Before payment, checkout calls the Fraud Scoring Service directly; a missing score does not block the order.
6. The payment is authorized by calling the Payments API (still called payment-service in some dashboards).
7. Finally the order is persisted by the Order Service, which writes to the Orders DB and confirms the stock reservation with Inventory.

## Failure behaviour

All calls on the critical path are synchronous HTTP with a 5 second budget. If payments are slow, checkout requests pile up behind them, so the checkout dashboard is usually the first place payment problems show up. Fraud scoring is soft: when it is unavailable the order continues without a score.

## Open questions

- Should fraud scoring move into the Payments domain? A proposal is being discussed with the Payments Team.
- Saved-address prefill depends on the Accounts Service API and is planned for Q3.
title: Checkout architecture overview

author: Kenji Watanabe
content:
# Data platform overview

_Owner: Data Platform Team._

The Event Bus (our Kafka cluster) is operated by the Data Platform Team, which also owns the Warehouse Loader.

## Event Bus

Three brokers, replication factor 3, seven-day retention on all topics. The Order Service publishes order lifecycle events to the topic order-events. More producers are expected after the planned migration of notifications and inventory.

## Warehouse Loader

The Warehouse Loader (dw loader / nightly ETL) feeds the analytics data warehouse - not to be confused with Warehouse Sync, which handles physical warehouse stock.

- It consumes events from the Event Bus for near-real-time tables.
- A nightly export reads order tables from the Orders DB; this export must always use the read replica.

## Ownership boundaries

Schema changes in the Orders DB must be announced to Data Platform at least one week in advance because the export queries depend on column names.
title: Data platform overview

author: Amara Okafor
content:
# Identity and authentication architecture

_Owner: Identity Team._

The Auth Service (our IdP) is run by the Identity Team, which also owns the Accounts Service.

## Sessions and tokens

The Auth Service issues a short-lived JWT and a refresh token at login. Session state is stored in the session shards of Shared Redis; if Redis loses keys, users are logged out. Tokens are signed with a key that is rotated manually every quarter.

## Who calls auth

- The API Gateway validates tokens with the Auth Service for every authenticated request.
- The Checkout API re-validates the session on each checkout step.

## Profile data

At login the Auth Service reads profile flags from the Accounts Service; this call is soft and login continues with defaults if Accounts is slow. The Accounts Service stores profiles, saved addresses and privacy export requests in its own database.

## Operational notes

Token validation is on the hot path of every request, so any latency added there is multiplied across the platform.
title: Identity and authentication architecture

author: Jonas Lindqvist
content:
# Inventory and catalog architecture

_Owner: Inventory Team. Updated after the August event bus migration._

The Inventory Service is owned by the Inventory Team, together with the Catalog Service and the Warehouse Sync worker.

Note: "warehouse" in this document means the physical fulfilment warehouse. The analytics data warehouse and its loader belong to Data Platform.

## Stock

The Inventory Service (stock service) is the source of truth for stock levels. Warehouse Sync pulls stock deltas from the partner WMS and pushes them into the Inventory Service. Checkout reserves stock synchronously and the Order Service confirms reservations when an order is created.

Since 5 August 2026 the Inventory Service also publishes stock-changed events to the Event Bus.

## Catalog

The Catalog Service holds product data, images and the search index. It uses Shared Redis as a read-through cache and consumes stock updates from Inventory asynchronously to show availability badges. The catalog is exposed to clients through the API Gateway.

## Pitfalls

- A cold catalog cache turns every pricing request into a catalog database read.
- Stock snapshots must never overwrite newer counts.
title: Inventory and catalog architecture

author: Sofia Marquez
content:
# Customer notifications architecture

_Owner: Customer Comms Team. Revised 10 August 2026._

The Notification Service (notifier) is owned by Customer Comms, as is the Email Dispatcher.

## Event intake

Since 5 August 2026 the notifier consumes order lifecycle events from the Event Bus topic order-events. Until that date it received the same events through an HTTP webhook called by the Order Service. The webhook has been switched off and will be deleted.

## Sending

For every notification the notifier enqueues a message for the Email Dispatcher (mailer), which renders the template and hands it to MailRelay for delivery. Retries carry an idempotency key so duplicates are dropped by the mailer.

## Limits

MailRelay enforces an hourly quota per account. Campaign days need a quota increase requested in advance.
title: Customer notifications architecture

author: Tomasz Wierzbicki
content:
# Payments platform architecture

_Updated 20 July 2026 after fraud scoring moved into the payment flow. Owner: Payments Team._

## Components

| Component | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Payments API (pay-api) | Public payment entry point used by checkout |
| Fraud Scoring Service | ML risk score per transaction |
| PSP Adapter | Talks to the PayNova card processor |
| Ledger Service | Double-entry bookkeeping |

The Payments API is owned by the Payments Team, as is the PSP Adapter.

## Authorization path

Checkout API calls pay-api synchronously to authorize a card payment. Since 1 June 2026, the Payments API calls the Fraud Scoring Service before every authorization; before that date checkout called fraud scoring itself. pay-api then forwards the authorization to the PSP Adapter, which calls the PayNova API. PayNova is currently our only card processor.

## Persistence

Payment records live in the payments schema of the shared Orders DB (pg-orders). Each pay-api pod keeps its own connection pool to pg-orders; pool sizing matters because the database is shared with the Order Service and the Ledger Service.

Captures and refunds are sent to the Ledger Service asynchronously through a queue, so a slow ledger does not block checkout. The ledger also stores its entries in the Orders DB.

## Known risks

- Single card processor; no failover.
- Shared database: a heavy query from any of the three payment-adjacent services can starve the others.
- The legacy hostname payment-service was removed in v3.0.0, but older runbooks and dashboards still use it.
title: Payments platform architecture

author: Hannah Becker
content:
# Shared infrastructure overview

_Owner: Platform SRE._

Platform SRE owns the API Gateway, the Orders DB cluster and Shared Redis.

## API Gateway (edge)

Envoy-based edge for web and mobile. Terminates TLS, applies rate limits and routes to the Checkout API and the Catalog Service. Authenticated routes call the Auth Service to validate tokens.

## Orders DB (pg-orders)

PostgreSQL 16 primary with one streaming read replica. Despite the name it is shared: orders, payments and ledger schemas all live here. Clients: Order Service, Payments API, Ledger Service and Warehouse Loader (replica only). max_connections is 600.

## Shared Redis (cache cluster)

Redis 7 with separate shards for sessions, carts and general caches. Users: Auth Service sessions, Cart Service carts and Catalog Service cache. Persistence is disabled by default because most data is cache.
title: Shared infrastructure overview

content:
# Staging load test report - spring campaign readiness

Environment: **staging**, 28 March 2026. Target: 3x the 2025 peak checkout rate.

## Results

| Step | 1x | 2x | 3x |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Checkout success | 99.8% | 99.5% | 91.2% |
| p95 checkout latency | 0.9 s | 1.4 s | 4.8 s |

## Findings

1. **Connection pool exhaustion in the payments service at 3x.** The staging payment-service pods are configured with only 10 database connections each, half the production value. At 3x load the pool was exhausted and requests waited for a connection. This is a staging configuration artefact, not a production risk, but staging should mirror production pool sizes.
2. The staging database instance reached 70% CPU at 3x; production has more headroom.
3. Inventory stock checks stayed below 120 ms at all load levels with the current one-call-per-cart design.

## Recommendation

The platform is ready for the spring campaign at 2x. Raise staging pool sizes to production values before the next test.
title: Staging load test report - spring campaign readiness

content:
# Incident severity and on-call policy

## Severity levels

| Level | Definition | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SEV1 | Critical. Customers cannot buy, pay or log in at scale. | Checkout failing for more than 25% of attempts |
| SEV2 | Major. Significant customer impact or data correctness problem. | Wrong charges, large-scale overselling |
| SEV3 | Minor. Limited customer impact with a workaround. | Slow profile updates |
| SEV4 | Low. Cosmetic or internal-only impact. | Stale analytics dashboards |

SEV1 and SEV2 incidents are called **severe** incidents and always require a written postmortem within five working days. SEV3 and SEV4 incidents are closed with a short resolution note on the incident ticket.

## Roles

- **Incident commander** - coordinates, does not debug.
- **Communications lead** - status page and Support updates for SEV1/SEV2.
- **Subject matter experts** - the on-call engineers of the affected services.

## Change freeze

No production releases on Fridays after 15:00 UTC or during declared SEV1 incidents, except rollbacks and fixes for the incident itself.

## Postmortems

Postmortems are blameless. The root cause section must name the verified cause; early hypotheses from the incident channel belong in the timeline, not in the root cause.

# Postmortem: INC-102 - Users logged out and unable to sign in

Date: 9 April 2026 | Authors: Identity Team | Status: Final

## Summary
Customers were randomly signed out, including in the middle of checkout, and some could not log back in.
INC-102 was a SEV2 incident with Auth Service as the primary service. Impact started at 13:05 UTC on 9 April 2026, was mitigated at 15:20 UTC and the incident was resolved at 16:45 UTC on 9 April 2026 (total 3 h 40 min).

## Customer impact
For about two hours roughly one in five active sessions was dropped. Customers lost their place in checkout and had to log in again; around 9% of login attempts failed with a generic error.
Affected services: Auth Service (primary), Shared Redis (degraded), checkout service (downstream), API Gateway (downstream)

## Timeline (UTC)
- 13:12 - AuthSessionMissRateHigh alert fires.
- 13:40 - Identity on-call sees sessions missing from Shared Redis.
- 14:30 - evicted_keys counter found climbing on all shards.
- 15:20 - Eviction policy and memory limit changed; errors drop.
- 16:45 - Incident resolved after an hour of stable metrics.

## Root cause
The shared-redis shards were at their 8 GB memory limit and the allkeys-lru eviction policy started evicting live session keys, which have no TTL priority over cache entries. Traffic growth after the spring campaign pushed memory over the limit.
No deployment triggered this incident.

## Ruled out
The session key prefix change shipped in auth-service v6.0.0 was reviewed and is unrelated; keys were present until evicted.

## Resolution
Platform SRE switched the eviction policy to volatile-lru and doubled maxmemory to 16 GB per shard (the Shared Redis config change maxmemory-policy-volatile-lru); session loss stopped immediately after the change.

## Action items
- [ ] Separate the session cache from general caches
- [ ] Alert on Redis evicted_keys rate

# Postmortem: INC-104 - Card payments failing at checkout

Date: 22 April 2026 | Authors: Payments Team | Status: Final

## Summary
Customers could not complete purchases because payment requests timed out on the final checkout step.
INC-104 was a SEV1 incident with Payments API as the primary service. Impact started at 10:12 UTC on 22 April 2026, was mitigated at 11:05 UTC and the incident was resolved at 11:40 UTC on 22 April 2026 (total 1 h 28 min).

## Customer impact
Roughly 38% of card payment attempts failed for 53 minutes. Shoppers saw "Your payment could not be processed" on the last step of checkout and many abandoned their carts.
Affected services: payments-api (primary), Checkout API (downstream)

## Timeline (UTC)
- 09:40 - Cart Service v1.12.0 deployed.
- 10:05 - payments-api release 2.8.0 rollout starts.
- 10:12 - Payment timeouts begin.
- 10:19 - CheckoutPaymentErrorRate alert fires; incident declared SEV1.
- 10:35 - Cart Service rollback considered; dashboards show cart is healthy.
- 10:48 - DB pool metrics show all 10 connections in use on every payments pod.
- 11:02 - Rollback to v2.7.3 completed.
- 11:05 - Payment success rate back to baseline.

## Root cause
The configuration refactor in version 2.8.0 of payments-api read the database pool size from a new PAYMENTS_DB_POOL_MAX variable that was never set in production, so every pod fell back to the default of 10 connections instead of 40. Under normal morning traffic the connection pool was exhausted within minutes; authorization requests queued waiting for a free connection and timed out after five seconds.
Errors started seven minutes after version 2.8.0 of Payments API reached 100% of pods.

## Ruled out
The Cart Service release deployed at 09:40 was initially suspected because of its timing, but its error rates were flat and it does not touch the payment path. It was ruled out.

## Resolution
The Payments team rolled back to v2.7.3 at 11:02 (the rollback of payments-api to v2.7.3); pool utilisation fell below 50% and payment success returned to normal by 11:05. The fixed config was re-released two weeks later.

## Action items
- [ ] Fail startup when the pool is smaller than the worker count
- [ ] Add pool saturation alert for Payments API
- [ ] Config defaults reviewed by a second engineer

# Postmortem: INC-123 - Payments outage caused by orders database overload

Date: 17 August 2026 | Authors: Payments Team | Status: Final

## Summary
Payments failed and orders could not be placed while the orders database was pegged at 100% CPU.
INC-123 was a SEV1 incident with Payments API as the primary service. Impact started at 09:00 UTC on 17 August 2026, was mitigated at 10:15 UTC and the incident was resolved at 12:40 UTC on 17 August 2026 (total 3 h 40 min).

## Customer impact
For 75 minutes about 60% of checkouts failed, the largest outage of the quarter. Ledger postings were delayed but none were lost.
Affected services: Payments API (primary), primary postgres (degraded), payments ledger (degraded), Order Service (degraded), Checkout API (downstream)

## Timeline (UTC)
- 07:30 - version 5.6.0 of Checkout API deployed.
- 08:10 - version 3.1.0 of payments-api deployed.
- 09:00 - Finance dashboard begins polling the reconciliation endpoint.
- 09:04 - Database CPU and payment latency alerts; SEV1 declared.
- 09:40 - Top query traced to the reconciliation endpoint.
- 10:10 - recon_v2 flag disabled; CPU drops.
- 12:40 - Index added via hotfix.

## Root cause
The new settlement reconciliation endpoint in Payments API v3.1.0 ran a refund listing query without a supporting index. When the Finance dashboard started polling it at 09:00, each call scanned the full payments table on the Orders DB primary. CPU saturation slowed every query; payments, ledger and order-service connection pools were depleted and requests timed out.
Trigger: the Payments API v3.1.0 release.

## Ruled out
Checkout API release 5.6.0 was examined first because it shipped the same morning, but its traffic pattern was unchanged and its error rate followed the database, not the other way round. It was ruled out.

## Resolution
The recon_v2 feature flag was turned off at 10:10, which stopped the expensive query, and version 3.1.1 of payments backend added the missing index at 12:40. No rollback was needed.

## Action items
- [ ] Query plan review for new endpoints on the shared database
- [ ] Per-service statement timeouts on orders-db
- [ ] Rate limit for internal dashboard polling

content:
# Runbook: API Gateway (edge)

Owner: Platform SRE, #sre.

## Elevated 5xx

502s from the edge usually mean an upstream is down or a TLS problem with clients. Check the per-route upstream health first. For TLS handshake failures, confirm which certificate chain is being served (`openssl s_client -connect shop.kestrel.example:443 -showcerts`). Older mobile app versions pin the previous intermediate CA.

## 429 Too Many Requests

Rate limits are defined in the policy file. Keying by client IP is unsafe for mobile traffic behind carrier NAT. Revert the policy with `edgectl policy rollback`.

## Authentication

Every authenticated route calls the Auth Service. Slow token validation shows up as gateway latency on all routes at once.
title: Runbook: API Gateway

author: Mateo Silva
content:
# Runbook: Auth Service (identity service)

Owner: Identity Team, #team-identity.

## Alerts

- **AuthSessionMissRateHigh** - more than 2% of session lookups miss.
- **AuthErrorRate** - more than 1% failed logins with 5xx.
- **TokenValidationLatency** - p95 above 300 ms.

## Users being logged out

Sessions live in the Shared Redis session shards. If users are randomly logged out:

1. Check `evicted_keys` on the session shards. Any evictions mean Redis is out of memory and is dropping sessions.
2. Check for a recent failover of a session shard.
3. Do not flush the session shards - that logs out everyone.

## Token validation slow

Token validation must use the cached JWKS key set. If latency rises after a release, roll back first.

## Signing key expiry

The signing key is rotated quarterly by hand. If all tokens suddenly fail validation at a fixed time (often midnight UTC), check the key expiry: `authctl keys list`. Emergency rotation: `authctl keys rotate --emergency`.
title: Runbook: Auth Service

Owner: Inventory Team.

## Stale images or product data

Check the Cache-Control headers returned for the asset. Purge the CDN path with `cdnctl purge /img/thumbs/*`. Thumbnail URLs are not content-addressed, so long max-age values cause stale images.

## Cache miss storm

The catalog read-through cache lives in Shared Redis. After a Redis restart the cache is empty and every request hits the catalog database. Enable request coalescing (`CATALOG_COALESCE=true`) and warm the cache from the latest snapshot: `catalogctl cache warm --from-snapshot latest`.

## Search index

New products appear in search only after the index rebuild job runs. Check the job status in the scheduler and the `search_index_age_seconds` metric.

## Availability badges

Badges are cached separately for 10 minutes. If badges disagree with stock, flush the badge cache.
title: Runbook: Catalog Service

author: Daniel Kim
content:
# Runbook: Checkout API

Owner: Checkout Team, #team-checkout.

## Alerts

- **CheckoutSuccessRate** - fewer than 92% of started checkouts complete within 10 minutes.
- **Checkout5xxRate** - more than 1% HTTP 5xx responses.
- **CheckoutLatencyHigh** - p95 of any step above 2 s.

## First five minutes

Checkout fails whenever one of its synchronous dependencies fails, so start by finding which downstream call is slow:

| Downstream | Dashboard panel |
| --- | --- |
| Payments API | "payment authorize" span |
| Inventory Service | "stock check / reserve" span |
| Pricing Engine | "price quote" span |
| Cart Service | "load cart" span |

A failing payment step almost always means Payments API is unhealthy; switch to the Payments runbook. Stock check timeouts point to the Inventory Service - check its thread pool saturation and request queue.

## Our own releases

If errors started within 30 minutes of a co-api release, roll back first and investigate later: `deployctl rollback checkout-api --to <previous-version>`. Remember that a rollback does not drain queues in downstream services; a dependency may need a restart.

## Customer-facing messaging

If checkout success is below 80% for more than 10 minutes, ask Support to post the status banner.
title: Runbook: Checkout API

author: Kenji Watanabe
content:
# Runbook: Event Bus (Kafka cluster)

Owner: Data Platform Team, #team-data.

## Alerts

- **BrokerDiskUsage** - any broker data volume above 85%.
- **ConsumerLagHigh** - any consumer group more than 30 minutes behind.
- **UnderReplicatedPartitions** - more than 0 for 10 minutes.

## Consumer lag

1. Check whether lag is growing for one group or all groups.
2. Frequent rebalances (look for `Revoking partitions` in consumer logs) usually mean the session timeout is too short or consumers are slow to poll.
3. Raise `session.timeout.ms` to 45 s for slow consumers.

## Broker disk full

When disks fill, brokers stop accepting writes and producers start buffering. Free space by deleting old segments of high-volume topics (`kafka-configs --alter --add-config retention.ms=...`), then expand volumes.

## Consumers

Warehouse Loader and, since August, the Notification Service consume from the cluster; Order Service and Inventory Service produce to it.
title: Runbook: Event Bus (Kafka)

author: Elif Yilmaz
content:
# Runbook: Fraud Scoring Service (risk-scoring)

Owner: Payments Team, ML engineers on the risk rotation.

## Callers

Since 1 June the Payments API calls fraud scoring before each authorization. The previous direct call from checkout has been removed.

## Decline rate spike

1. Split declines by reason: "high risk" vs "score unavailable".
2. "score unavailable" means the caller timed out - check fraud p95 latency against the caller's timeout.
3. "high risk" spikes after a model or threshold change: roll back the model release.

## Signals

Account age and history are fetched from the Accounts Service. If Accounts is slow, scores are computed without these signals and become less accurate.
title: Runbook: Fraud Scoring Service

author: Jonas Lindqvist
content:
# Runbook: Inventory Service (stock service)

Owner: Inventory Team.

## Alerts

- **InventoryThreadPoolSaturation** - request worker pool more than 90% busy.
- **StockFreshness** - no stock update from the partner WMS for 60 minutes.
- **OversellDetector** - orders accepted for SKUs with zero stock.

## Thread pool saturation

The service has a fixed worker pool of 200 threads. When callers send many more stock checks than usual, requests queue and time out. Queued requests are not shed automatically, so after the excess traffic stops the pods may stay saturated; restart pods one zone at a time to clear the queue.

## Overselling

Stock updates come from Warehouse Sync. If the oversell detector fires, pause Warehouse Sync first (`deployctl scale warehouse-sync --replicas 0`), then compare stock with the WMS export and run the reconciliation script.

## Stale stock

Check the Warehouse Sync logs for 401 or 429 errors from the partner WMS.
title: Runbook: Inventory Service

author: Marta Kowalczyk
content:
# Runbook: Ledger Service

Owner: Payments Team (finance engineering rotation).

## Reconciliation mismatch

The nightly job compares the PayNova settlement file with ledger entries. A mismatch on refunds usually means double posting:

1. Query postings grouped by refund id with more than one row.
2. Check whether the idempotency key format changed recently.
3. Do not delete postings; Finance corrects them with reversal entries.

## Delayed postings

Payments API sends captures and refunds through a queue, so the ledger can fall behind without affecting checkout. The ledger writes to the Orders DB; if the database is saturated, postings queue up and are processed once it recovers.
title: Runbook: Ledger Service

author: Ahmed Hassan
content:
# Runbook: Notification Service (notifier)

Owner: Customer Comms Team.

## Alerts

- **EmailVolumeAnomaly** - sends per minute below 20% of the forecast.
- **NotifierPodRestarts** - more than 3 restarts in 15 minutes.
- **NotifierConsumerLag** - lag on the order-events consumer group above 5,000.

## No notifications being sent

Order events are consumed from the Event Bus topic order-events. Check that the consumer group is assigned partitions and that `NOTIFY_ORDER_TOPIC` is `order-events`. After fixing, replay missed events with `notifyctl replay --since <timestamp>`.

## Delayed emails

Messages are handed to the Email Dispatcher queue. If that queue grows, see the Email Dispatcher dashboard and check MailRelay 429 responses.

## OOM restarts

Look at heap usage per pod. Caches must be bounded.
title: Runbook: Notification Service

author: Hannah Becker
content:
# Runbook: Orders DB (pg-orders)

Owner: Platform SRE. The cluster is shared by orders, payments and ledger, so a problem here usually looks like a checkout or payments outage first.

## Alerts

- **OrdersDbActiveConnectionsHigh** - more than 480 of 600 connections in use.
- **OrdersDbCpuHigh** - primary CPU above 85% for 5 minutes.
- **ReplicaLagHigh** - replica more than 60 s behind.

## Database saturation

Signs: CPU or I/O pegged, many sessions in `active` state, clients reporting "too many connections" or connection checkout timeouts.

1. Find the heaviest sessions:
   `SELECT pid, usename, application_name, state, now() - query_start AS age, left(query, 80) FROM pg_stat_activity ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 20;`
2. Check `application_name`. Analytics jobs must never run on the primary - the Warehouse Loader is only allowed to read from the replica.
3. Cancel the offending query with `pg_cancel_backend(pid)`; terminate only if cancel fails.
4. Look for new queries without indexes (sequential scans on payments or orders tables) - recent releases of any of the three client services are suspects.

## Replica lag

Avoid VACUUM FULL or large index builds on the primary during business hours; they generate WAL bursts the replica cannot keep up with.

## Clients

Order Service, Payments API and Ledger Service write to the primary.
title: Runbook: Orders DB (pg-orders)

author: Oskar Nowak
content:
# Runbook: Payments API (payment-service)

Owner: Payments Team, #team-payments. Pager rotation: payments-primary.

## Alerts

- **PaymentAuthLatency** - p95 authorization latency above 1.5 s for 5 minutes.
- **PaymentsDbPoolSaturation** - more than 90% of database connections in use on any pod. Added after INC-104.
- **CheckoutPaymentErrorRate** - owned by Checkout but usually means a payments problem.

## Connection pool exhaustion

Symptoms: authorization requests time out after about 5 seconds, logs show `QueuePool limit reached` or `timeout waiting for connection`, and the pool gauge sits at its maximum.

1. Check `payments_db_pool_in_use` against `payments_db_pool_max` per pod. Every pod holds its own pool against pg-orders. The expected maximum is 40.
2. If the maximum is lower than 40, the pool size configuration is wrong - check `PAYMENTS_DB_POOL_MAX` and roll back the last release if it changed config.
3. If the pool is full but the maximum is correct, the database itself is probably slow. Look at the Orders DB runbook for saturation and long-running queries before scaling pay-api: adding pods adds connections and can make database saturation worse.

## PSP timeouts

Authorizations are forwarded to the PSP Adapter. If only the PSP call is slow, check the PSP Adapter dashboard and the PayNova status page. Client-side keep-alive and idle timeouts must be shorter than the adapter's (60 s).

## Fraud scoring

Fraud scoring has been called by pay-api since June. A slow fraud service shows up as "score unavailable" declines, not as timeouts.

## Rollback

`deployctl rollback payments-api --to <previous-version>`. A rollback takes about 3 minutes for all pods.
title: Runbook: Payments API

author: Tomasz Wierzbicki
content:
# Runbook: PSP Adapter (provider-gateway)

Owner: Payments Team.

## What it does

The adapter translates our payment requests into PayNova API calls, including the 3-D Secure redirect and return flow.

## Alerts

- **PspAuthorizationFailureRate** - more than 5% of authorizations rejected with a 5xx from PayNova.
- **PspThreeDsReturnErrors** - spike in 404s on the 3DS return path.

## PayNova outage

1. Check the PayNova status page and the #vendor-paynova channel.
2. Compare our error codes: HTTP 503 from PayNova means the processor is down; there is nothing to roll back on our side.
3. Ask Support to suggest PayPal or gift cards. We currently have no secondary card processor.

## 3-D Secure return path

Callback URLs are registered with each acquirer at PayNova. Never change the return path without registering the new URL for every acquirer first, and keep the old path as an alias for at least a week.

## Keep-alive

The adapter closes idle client connections after 60 seconds. Clients must use a shorter idle timeout.
title: Runbook: PSP Adapter

author: Hannah Becker
content:
# Runbook: Shared Redis (cache cluster)

Owner: Platform SRE.

## Shards

| Shard group | Used by | Persistence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sessions | Auth Service | AOF since June |
| carts | Cart Service | AOF since June |
| cache | Catalog Service, misc | none |

## Memory pressure

Watch `used_memory` against `maxmemory` and the `evicted_keys` counter. The eviction policy is volatile-lru so keys without a TTL are never evicted; if memory still fills, scale the shard rather than changing the policy.

## Failover

A failover of the sessions shard logs users out if persistence is off. After any failover check key counts against the previous day.

## Maintenance

Rolling restarts empty the cache shards. Warm the catalog cache before returning a shard to service and avoid restarts between 05:00 and 09:00 UTC (APAC peak).
title: Runbook: Shared Redis

author: Ravi Menon
content:
# Runbook: Warehouse Loader (dw loader)

Owner: Data Platform Team. Not to be confused with Warehouse Sync (physical warehouse stock, Inventory Team).

## Failed nightly load

1. Open the Airflow DAG `orders_daily` and read the failing task log.
2. `column ... does not exist` means an upstream schema change; update the column mapping.
3. Backfill with `airflow dags backfill orders_daily -s <date> -e <date>`.

## Export source

The nightly export reads from the Orders DB - always through the replica endpoint `pg-orders-replica`. After any replica rebuild, verify the connection string; pointing at the primary can saturate the production database.

## Streaming tables

Near-real-time tables are fed from the Event Bus. If counts look inflated, check the producing service for duplicate events before blaming the loader.
title: Runbook: Warehouse Loader (nightly ETL)

author: Amara Okafor
content:
# Authentication security review - H1 2026

## Scope

Token issuance and validation in the Auth Service, session storage, and edge token checks.

## Findings

1. **Manual signing key rotation (medium).** The JWT signing key is rotated by hand every quarter using a calendar reminder. There is no alert before expiry. Recommendation: automate rotation and alert 14 days before expiry. Status: accepted, not yet scheduled.
2. **JWKS caching (low).** Validators cache the key set indefinitely. A planned change will refresh it more often.
3. **Password reset rate limiting (resolved).** Added in v6.1.4.

## Out of scope

Third-party identity providers and the mobile app's certificate pinning.
title: Authentication security review - H1 2026

# INC-120: Order status page showing stale data

Severity: SEV3 | Status: Resolved | Primary service: primary postgres
Opened: 2026-07-30 12:10 UTC (impact started 11:00 UTC)
Affected services: Orders DB (primary), Order Service (degraded), warehouse-loader (downstream)

## Description
Customers saw outdated order statuses because the read replica fell behind.

## Impact
The order tracking page showed statuses up to 40 minutes old for four hours; support handled extra "where is my order" contacts.

## Detection
ReplicaLagHigh alert.

## Initial notes from the incident channel
Network issue between availability zones.

## Resolution note
Cause: An aggressive manual VACUUM FULL on a large audit table on the orders-db primary generated a burst of WAL that the replica could not apply fast enough.
The vacuum was cancelled and rescheduled for a low-traffic window with throttling; replication caught up by 16:30.
Resolved: 2026-07-30 16:30 UTC
title: INC-120: Order status page showing stale data

# INC-122: Duplicated stock events inflate analytics

Severity: SEV4 | Status: Resolved | Primary service: Inventory Service
Opened: 2026-08-11 09:00 UTC (impact started 07:00 UTC)
Affected services: Inventory Service (primary), warehouse-loader (downstream)

## Description
Analytics showed stock movements roughly doubled since early August.

## Impact
Inventory analytics were wrong for a week. Actual stock levels were correct.

## Detection
An analyst noticed stock movement counts far above order volume.

## Initial notes from the incident channel
Warehouse loader reading the topic twice.

## Resolution note
Cause: The producer introduced in the Inventory Service v3.6.0 release retried on timeouts without idempotence, publishing many stock-changed events twice.
inventory-service v3.6.1 added deterministic event ids and idempotent producer retries; analytics were rebuilt.

# INC-123: Payments outage caused by orders database overload

Severity: SEV1 | Status: Resolved | Primary service: payments-api
Opened: 2026-08-17 09:04 UTC (impact started 09:00 UTC)
Affected services: payments-api (primary), orders-db (degraded), Ledger Service (degraded), Order Service (degraded), Checkout API (downstream)

## Description
Payments failed and orders could not be placed while the orders database was pegged at 100% CPU.

## Impact
For 75 minutes about 60% of checkouts failed, the largest outage of the quarter. Ledger postings were delayed but none were lost.

## Detection
OrdersDbCpuHigh and PaymentAuthLatency alerts fired within a minute of each other at 09:04.

## Initial notes from the incident channel
The checkout-api v5.6.0 express checkout release at 07:30 could be increasing load on payments.

## Resolution note
The recon_v2 feature flag was turned off at 10:10, which stopped the expensive query, and Payments API release 3.1.1 added the missing index at 12:40. No rollback was needed.
Full analysis in the postmortem DOC-PM-INC-123.
Resolved: 2026-08-17 12:40 UTC
title: INC-123: Payments outage caused by orders database overload

content:
# INC-125: Mobile app users rate-limited

Severity: SEV3 | Status: Resolved | Primary service: API Gateway
Opened: 2026-08-29 13:20 UTC (impact started 13:02 UTC)
Affected services: edge (primary)

## Description
Many mobile users received "Too many requests" errors.

## Impact
About 14% of mobile requests were rejected with HTTP 429 for an hour, mostly from users on carrier networks sharing IP addresses.

## Detection
429 rate alert at the edge.

## Initial notes from the incident channel
Bot traffic.

## Resolution note
Cause: Rate limit policy v7 (the API Gateway config change rl-policy-v7) keyed limits by client IP. Mobile carriers place thousands of users behind shared NAT addresses, so they shared one bucket.
Reverted to policy v6 (the rollback of API Gateway to rl-policy-v6).
Resolved: 2026-08-29 14:05 UTC
title: INC-125: Mobile app users rate-limited

# INC-127: Fraud model false positives decline good customers

Severity: SEV3 | Status: Resolved | Primary service: Fraud Scoring Service
Opened: 2026-09-09 13:00 UTC (impact started 09:10 UTC)
Affected services: Fraud Scoring Service (primary), payments-api (downstream)

## Description
Fraud declines tripled after the new fraud model went live.

## Impact
About 1.8% of payments were wrongly declined as fraudulent for seven hours.

## Detection
Fraud decline rate dashboard reviewed by the Payments team.

## Initial notes from the incident channel
Model v24 is over-sensitive.

## Resolution note
Cause: fraud-service release 2.4.0 combined a new model with a lower decline threshold (0.85 instead of 0.92); the combination flagged many legitimate first-time customers.
Rolled back to v2.3.2 (the rollback of Fraud Scoring Service to v2.3.2); the model was re-released later with the old threshold.
Resolved: 2026-09-09 16:30 UTC
title: INC-127: Fraud model false positives decline good customers

Stock levels from the partner warehouse stopped updating overnight.

# INC-130: Order cancellations stuck in pending

Severity: SEV3 | Status: Resolved | Primary service: OMS
Opened: 2026-09-27 08:30 UTC (impact started 17:10 UTC)
Affected services: Order Service (primary), Payments API (downstream)

## Description
Customer-requested cancellations stayed in "cancellation pending" and refunds were not triggered.

870 cancellations were stuck overnight; refunds were delayed by up to 18 hours.

Support escalation.

Payments refund API failing.

# INC-132: Notification service restarting repeatedly

Severity: SEV3 | Status: Resolved | Primary service: notifications
Opened: 2026-10-06 14:30 UTC (impact started 14:00 UTC)
Affected services: Notification Service (primary)

## Description
Notification pods were repeatedly killed for running out of memory, delaying emails by minutes.

## Impact
Notifications were delayed by up to 20 minutes during restarts; none were lost.

## Detection
Pod restart alert.

## Initial notes from the incident channel
Memory leak in the event bus client.

## Resolution note
Cause: The in-memory template cache added in version 4.2.0 of notifications was unbounded and grew with every personalised template variant until pods hit their memory limit.

# INC-133: Checkout outage after new checkout release

Severity: SEV1 | Status: Resolved | Primary service: Checkout API
Opened: 2026-10-12 08:24 UTC (impact started 08:20 UTC)
Affected services: Checkout API (primary), Inventory Service (degraded), Order Service (downstream)

## Description
Most customers could not get through checkout after the new single-page checkout launched.

## Impact
For 95 minutes about 70% of checkout attempts failed or timed out. Orders that did go through were correct.

## Detection
CheckoutSuccessRate alert at 08:24.

## Initial notes from the incident channel
The Inventory Service is down.

## Resolution note
The release was rolled back to v5.7.1 at 09:10 (the rollback of Checkout API to v5.7.1). The rollback alone was only partially effective; inventory pods remained saturated with queued requests until they were restarted at 09:50, after which checkout success returned to normal at 09:55.
Full analysis in the postmortem DOC-PM-INC-133.
Resolved: 2026-10-12 10:30 UTC
title: INC-133: Checkout outage after new checkout release

# INC-134: Cart and checkout totals disagree by one cent

Severity: SEV3 | Status: Resolved | Primary service: Pricing Engine
Opened: 2026-10-15 15:00 UTC (impact started 10:10 UTC)
Affected services: pricing-service (primary), Cart Service (downstream), checkout service (downstream)

## Description
Some carts showed a total one cent different from the checkout total, and a few payments were rejected for amount mismatch.

## Impact
About 0.4% of checkouts were blocked by an amount mismatch error for 26 hours.

## Detection
Support reports of "total changed" errors.

## Initial notes from the incident channel
Currency conversion rates outdated.

## Resolution note
Cause: pricing-service release 2.7.0 moved rounding to line level using half-up rounding while the Cart Service used banker's rounding, producing one-cent differences.
version 2.7.1 of pricing aligned rounding with the Cart Service.

# INC-135: Event bus brokers out of disk

Severity: SEV2 | Status: Resolved | Primary service: Event Bus
Opened: 2026-10-20 11:34 UTC (impact started 11:30 UTC)
Affected services: Event Bus (primary), Notification Service (downstream), Warehouse Loader (downstream), Order Service (degraded), Inventory Service (degraded)

## Description
Order and stock events stopped flowing when Kafka brokers ran out of disk, delaying notifications.

## Impact
For about 100 minutes order notifications were not sent and stock events were not published; producers buffered and retried, so no events were lost.

## Detection
BrokerDiskUsage alert.

## Initial notes from the incident channel
Duplicate stock events filling disks again.

## Resolution note
Retention on high-volume topics was cut to 48 hours and broker volumes were expanded (the event-bus config change retention-48h).

# INC-138: Privacy data exports taking days

Severity: SEV3 | Status: Monitoring | Primary service: Accounts Service
Opened: 2026-10-30 08:00 UTC (impact started 08:00 UTC)
Affected services: accounts-service (primary)

## Description
Customer data export requests were taking several days instead of minutes.

## Impact
About 140 privacy export requests were delayed; the legal response deadline was not breached.

## Detection
Privacy team report.

## Initial notes from the incident channel
Export worker crashed.

## Resolution note
Cause: The export queue query in the accounts had no index on status and requested_at, and the table had grown to 40 million rows.
An index was added in Accounts Service release 1.5.1; the team is monitoring the backlog before closing the incident.
Mitigated: 2026-10-31 11:00 UTC; still being monitored.
title: INC-138: Privacy data exports taking days

# Secondary card processor evaluation (draft)

**Status:** draft - no decision yet.

## Why

The June PayNova outage showed that a single card processor is a single point of failure for checkout. This document compares options for a secondary processor that the PSP Adapter could fail over to.

## Shortlist

| Criterion | Vendor A | Vendor B | Vendor C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EU acquiring | yes | yes | partial |
| Network tokens | yes | no | yes |
| Integration effort | 6 weeks | 4 weeks | 8 weeks |

Vendor names are withheld until procurement signs NDAs.

## Next steps

- Commercial terms from all three vendors.
- Decision meeting to be scheduled; target Q4.
title: Secondary card processor evaluation (draft)
